speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: asked the Minister for Trade and Industry what is the current state of Singapore's economy and the growth risks ahead and where does the Government intend to pivot to, given this period of great external uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Key uncertainties include (a) the United States (US)-China trade dispute, which has gone beyond retaliatory tariffs to other areas, including restrictions on technology access and sales; (b) the uncertainty and risk of a disorderly Brexit; and (c) the political uncertainties of some regional economies.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: All these have dampened consumer and business confidence.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Lower demand in our key export markets has, in turn, affected our outward-oriented sectors, such as electronics, precision engineering and wholesale trade, whose performance remains weak.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Although the Economic Development Board (EDB) is on track to achieving its foreign investment targets for this year, we are watching businesses' investment decisions very closely.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: However, there are pockets of strength in our economy.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The information and communications sector is expected to grow, given firms’ robust demand for information technology and digital solutions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The education, health and social services sector is similarly expected to remain resilient.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The construction sector has also turned around after three years of contraction.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: MTI will review our forecast in August, taking into account the full set of economic data for the second quarter, as well as the latest external economic conditions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The medium-term outlook for the Singapore economy will be determined by the following factors.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Further tariffs will impact more goods and bring about even greater reorganisation of global supply chains.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Both countries' agreement to resume trade negotiations is welcome news, but there are fundamental disagreements between them and those will take time to resolve.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Prolonged US-China tensions will further undermine global business and consumer confidence.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, our medium-term outlook will depend on how our major export markets perform.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Southeast Asia remains a bright spark, and the US economy appears to be holding up.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: However, China's economy could slow down more sharply than expected due to the trade conflict with the US and this could further dampen its import demand from the region.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And Europe needs a decisive resolution on Brexit.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: While we must weather these immediate challenges, we must, more importantly, navigate more fundamental shifts in the global economy that will shape our medium- to long-term prospects.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: One is the future of the multilateral trading system.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Over the past 40 years, Singapore has benefited from increased economic integration and free trade, underpinned by international rules that apply to countries big and small, and anchored by the World Trade Organization (WTO).

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Unfortunately, the multilateral trading system is currently under stress.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The risks of economic balkanisation, where markets are bifurcated and trade, talent and data flows are disrupted, have grown.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: An increasingly protectionist global environment would reduce our access to markets.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When we are all reduced to competing for a slice of a shrinking economic pie, no one wins.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The second is the emergence of global rules that may affect our status as a global trading hub.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For instance, ongoing discussions to introduce minimum effective tax rates across countries will affect our competitiveness and carbon caps will constrain our growth potential.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We must navigate this carefully to preserve our economic space.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The third is our ability to harness our new technologies and create opportunities, especially in the digital economy.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: To overcome these challenges and seize the opportunities, we will focus our economic strategy on three prongs: first, strengthen our fundamentals to distinguish ourselves from the competition; second, create opportunities by constantly refreshing our offerings to business and investors; and third, promote a conducive global and regional business environment with like-minded countries and companies.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our fundamentals that have put us in good stead include the following: First, a stable political environment with a competent and united leadership.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, a pro-business environment, including rule of law, a pro-innovation regulatory environment, and a safe harbour for talent and ideas.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Third, superior connectivity in supply chains and distribution networks, spanning the physical dimensions like air, land and sea, and including the non-physical dimensions of data, finance, talent, technology and rules.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Fourth, a skilled workforce that continues to upgrade itself through training and retraining.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Fifth, a progressive tripartite partnership that enables the Government, businesses and labour to overcome our challenges together.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We must, however, extend our lead, by continuing to build on these fundamentals and seizing new opportunities.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As a small, open economy, Singapore must always adapt to changing external circumstances, and harness the power of our people and technology.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are making encouraging progress transforming our industries through the work of the Future Economy Council (FEC) and the Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs).

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our strong manufacturing sector will allow us to plug into global supply chains to meet demand from emerging adjacent industries, such as electric vehicles.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will build the next-generation industrial and technological estates, such as the Jurong Innovation District (JID) and the Punggol Digital District.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will also redevelop entire tracts at Sungei Kadut and Kranji for new industries.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: To enrich our tourism offerings, we are rejuvenating the two Integrated Resorts, transforming Orchard Road and exploring a tourism site at Jurong Lake District.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will also be developing Mandai and the Greater Southern Waterfront.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These initiatives will enhance our position as a global city for business and leisure.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Beyond transforming existing sectors and industries, we are also developing brand new sectors.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Innovation Park will bring together high-tech precision farming and research and development (R&D) activities, including indoor plant factories, insect farms and animal feed production facilities.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This will create a completely new range of jobs in agriculture and give a new generation of young technopreneur farmers the platform to commercialise their ideas.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Another new area that we are focusing on is Precision Medicine.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This uses each patient's biological data to more precisely predict, diagnose and treat diseases.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: EDB is working hard to bring to Singapore various biotech firms, medical technology firms and digital health players.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I have just opened Glaxo Smith Kline's (GSK's) two new manufacturing facilities last week.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: GSK's investment reflects their continued confidence in Singapore's future.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Besides transforming entire sectors, we will also support our companies to better harness the regional and global opportunities.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We already have a vibrant startup sector at Block 71, one-north.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But we can do a better job helping our companies scale up and grow.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We must also continue to work hard to translate our R&D capabilities into new business opportunities with our companies.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And there is no lack of opportunities and possibilities in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We can only be constrained by our imagination.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: To realise all these plans, we will continue to do our part to promote a conducive global and regional business environment with like-minded countries and companies.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is the third prong of our economic strategy.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is a key driver of our future economic growth.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will continue to advocate for an integrated, global digital economy.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This includes our efforts to co-develop international trade rules for the digital economy.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is the reason why we are co-convenors of the Joint Statement Initiative on E-commerce (JSI) at the WTO which has since attracted participation from 78 countries.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are also pursuing a pathfinder Digital Economy Partnership Agreement with Chile and New Zealand, and we are working with Australia on digital economy initiatives, which will all help to provide greater opportunities for our businesses in an increasingly digitalised future.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will also continue to strengthen and deepen and diversify our trade links.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will forge new partnerships through ongoing negotiations in the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP), as we call it, and the Pacific Alliance Free Trade Agreement (FTA).

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The potential for Singapore businesses will be enormous.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: At the same time, we will also review and upgrade our current partnerships, including the China-Singapore FTA, and the Comprehensive Economic Cooperation Agreement (CECA) with India.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These upgrades will increase the benefits that Singapore companies already gain from the existing FTAs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Today, more than 90% of Singapore's trade is covered by our various FTAs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These efforts will ensure that our external linkages remain strong whatever happens elsewhere in the world.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And collectively, they will give Team Singapore the best chance for success.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As Members can see, we are closely monitoring economic developments.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: While there are clouds looming, we believe we have the fundamentals to weather the storm.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are in a strong fiscal position, and we are making good progress in restructuring our economy.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Government also stands ready to step up our support for companies and workers in sustaining our core capabilities, enhancing our competitiveness to seize new opportunities.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, let us work together, plant the seeds for tomorrow's growth, till the land, and we should have a good harvest.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Notwithstanding the Minister's very reassuring reply, I still have two further questions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Indeed, the way things are developing, the world may, indeed, be trading less with one another, or investing less with one another as well, and both are important.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Trade and investments are always the key drivers for the Singapore economy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, I want to ask the Minister: should we be concerned that more economies around the world are becoming more nationalistic, governments are increasingly looking at balance of trade, current account balances as a pure zero-sum game?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How can tiny Singapore respond to this rising economic nationalism?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Can Singapore break out from this traditional C+I+G+X kind of model of growth?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The concern will be that there will not just be a shift in the supply chains or the distribution networks or the production sites.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The greater concern will be a general fall in investor and consumer confidence.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But this is something that we must do in the face of a potential fragmentation of the global economy.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On the Member's second question, as any economics student will know the GDP equation of C+I+G+X-M, that is, for GDP.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: How must Singapore grow our economy, going forward?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: What the Member is alluding to, if I read him correctly, is that we must not just look at what is happening domestically in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There are three things that we should be focused on.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: How do we help our companies and workers to build real capabilities in order to contest in the new world environment?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: How do we help them access markets; how do we make sure that the rules allow our companies to overcome both the tariff and the non-tariff barriers?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, that is the first part of how we need to run our economy.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The second part of how we need to run our economy goes beyond the GDP equation that we just mentioned.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And we talked about the gross national product (GNP).

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: How do we have a sizeable base of companies that operate beyond Singapore but contributing back to the Singapore economy?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And I will use the example of PSA.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Once upon a time, we believed that the port is critical to Singapore and we continue to believe so.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: One is to promote trade with a particular country.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The other – most ports are like that – they serve the local domestic economy.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But there is a second way of looking at the port, which is the way the Singapore port has developed.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are an exchange platform so that people do not just trade with Singapore; people trade through Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, even if the goods do not come to Singapore or come through Singapore, they will trade on the PSA platform or on the Singapore platform.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is a new way of looking at how we should do business.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is why Enterprise Singapore (ESG), together with the rest of our economic agencies, is spending so much effort to help our companies to use the world as our hinterland and never be constrained by our geographical size or geographical location.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And that will be the next lap of our economic development, and that will be one way where we break the conventional paradigm of the GDP equation which Mr Liang mentioned C+I+G+X-M.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The third prong which we must always bear in mind and, sometimes, not so obvious in the public consciousness in our economic strategy, will be how we manage our Reserves and where we put our investments.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This has given the Singapore economy a significant boost and helped our budgetary constraints very much.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And thus, we must continue to harness our Reserves judiciously to make sure that we create the biggest positive impact for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think the Minister highlighted the importance of strengthening the fundamentals in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One is related to something more detailed, in particular, the recent US Department of Commerce's proposed export controls on 14 categories of technology.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And I think it has some impact on Singapore, in particular, what the Minister mentioned, in terms of investments as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, whether the Minister can share with the House whether there would be a potential impact on Singapore, in terms of investments and potential tech-related restrictions that the US imposes on China, and how that affects Singapore companies as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The second is: the Minister highlighted about the trade and tech diversions and the supply chain changes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the region, other countries are also putting in efforts to pull in some of these trade diversions into their countries.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Minister share EDB's strategies, in terms of reaping some of the benefits, or pulling some of these production networks into Singapore, if any?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In the short term, various companies and countries may be able to take measures to shift their production or supply chains elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If that happens, then we are all the worse for it because it means that the global production system cannot be optimised as a whole, but it will be sub-optimised in parts.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This will lead to increased costs, a fragmented production chain and so forth.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But we must also inspire confidence in people who put their investments here that, even in such a world, we are able to manage the different sensitivities across different countries properly.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On the Member's second part about the shifts in the global supply chain, indeed, to use a very specific example, some people have said that various productions and supply chains have shifted out from China in the global reorganisation of that product chain.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There are some things that we do much better; there are some things that will not be re-allocated here.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The simple example is this: for what we call the low-mix, high-volume production, most of them will not come to Singapore because they compete on the basis of scale, labour costs, land costs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But what will come to Singapore will be what we call the high-mix, low-volume.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is where trust, standards, quality, assurance, intellectual property (IP) protection will become very important.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And we have seen more of such investments siting in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, just to give an example, last week, I went to GSK to open the new facilities.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Today's precision medicine is no longer just producing high volume at low cost.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Those kinds of medicine and drugs will probably shift to other countries where there is a cost-competitive advantage.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But GSK will be very keen to work with EDB to site their high-mix, low-volume pharmaceutical products in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Because for such high-mix, low-volume production, they require speed to market.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Which means that your supply chain, your distribution networks must be robust.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That, we do better than most other countries.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For such industries, it will require a strong IP regime where people can enforce their IP.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For such productions to happen in small batches, high volume, you require a certain agility in your regulatory framework, which we also do well.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, there are and there will be sectors that will play to Singapore's advantage.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But it does not mean that everything that moves out of China or moves out of India will necessarily come to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: [Pursuant to Standing Order No 22(3), provided that Members had not asked for questions standing in their names to be postponed to a later Sitting day or withdrawn, written answers to questions not reached by the end of Question Time are reproduced in the Appendix.]
